title: A coherent gamma-ray source

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reproducible beam of gamma rays at MeV photon energies with demonstrated longitudinal coherence: a measurable phase relationship in the radiation over a reported time or distance. The advance would make high-energy light available for controlled interference experiments. Brightness and a narrow forward beam are useful properties, but neither establishes this coherence. Stimulated amplification or spectral narrowing would also require additional evidence connecting the observation to the claimed phase coherence.

Two distinct routes share this output goal. A nuclear gamma-ray laser, often called a graser, would obtain amplification through stimulated nuclear emission. A gamma-ray free-electron laser would generate radiation through electron dynamics; achieving that source would not itself demonstrate stimulated nuclear emission. The supplied sources describe theoretical nuclear schemes and an electron–laser research program pursuing these possibilities, rather than demonstrated devices meeting the proposed criterion.

Scope synthesis: MeV energy is an explicit boundary for this record, not a definition of all gamma radiation or all nuclear transitions. The concept does not depend on claiming that nuclear radiation is invariably spontaneous and incoherent. Its defining requirement is a source with measured longitudinal coherence in the stated energy regime, together with reproducible operation.

significance.text: A successful source would extend controlled light-source physics into a demanding high-energy regime. The useful analogy with optical lasers is the ability to control and exploit coherence, which helped turn light into a precise experimental and technological tool. Demonstrating longitudinal coherence at MeV energies would directly support interference experiments with that radiation. It would not, by itself, reproduce the full range of capabilities or applications of visible-light lasers.

Coherent nuclear spectroscopy and imaging of dense objects are technically motivated applications. Nuclear spectroscopy would additionally require access to suitable resonances and usable beam properties. Practical radiography would require adequate photon flux, illumination geometry and detection performance. Rochester's research announcement identifies nuclear studies and dense-material imaging as motivations, but provides no demonstration that these applications have been achieved with a coherent MeV source. They are conditional consequences of further source development, rather than automatic results of the minimum coherence demonstration.

Impact boundary synthesis: coherence alone does not establish a practical directed-energy system, intense antimatter production or a new source of power. Such outcomes would require separate advances and evidence concerning beam energy, efficiency, interaction mechanisms and operating conditions. They are outside the direct impact claimed for this innovation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reproducible production of MeV gamma radiation whose longitudinal coherence is established experimentally and whose extent is reported. An intense bremsstrahlung or inverse-Compton source would not meet that requirement merely by producing more photons or concentrating them into a forward cone. The supplied literature motivates coherent gamma sources as a research goal, but does not establish the field's complete status as of November 1, 2026.

For nuclear schemes, the graser dilemma involves the difficulty of reconciling available pumping power against spontaneous decay with the stimulated-emission cross section needed for amplification. Small cross sections and demanding excitation conditions make useful gain difficult. Additional barriers include recoil, resonance broadening and survival of the target under intense pumping. These constraints interact: a pump capable of producing the required excited population can also disturb the narrow resonance conditions on which the proposed amplification depends.

Solid-state Mössbauer approaches seek to exploit recoil-free resonances, but the supplied material does not document a working graser from such a scheme. The retained multi-photon proposal instead investigates laser-plasma gamma flashes and intense auxiliary photons as possible ways around nuclear amplification constraints. Its proposed mechanisms and operating conditions remain theoretical; explaining a route around a barrier does not demonstrate that the required gain, coherence and target behavior can coexist experimentally.

The electron route presents a separate engineering and physics challenge. Rochester's program proposes studying coherence in radiation emitted when electrons interact with a strong laser field, with a gamma-ray free-electron laser as a possible eventual outcome. Establishing the underlying radiation coherence is an initial research objective; building a reproducible source with the specified photon energy and measured coherence would require further progress beyond that study.

current_state.text: The retained Yang–Spohr–Doria arXiv preprint presents theoretical multi-photon stimulated-emission schemes using laser-plasma gamma flashes and intense auxiliary photons. It identifies ELI-NP's multi-petawatt laser platform as a possible setting for pursuing these designs. It reports no experimental graser. The supplied review assessed the complete retained prose, with no reported text-extraction truncation, but did not inspect the figures; the qualitative account of the proposal rests on explicit statements in the text.

The preprint's chronology requires qualification. Its header identifies arXiv:2404.10025v1 dated April 15, 2024, while the retained body also displays August 24, 2026. The supplied evidence does not explain this discrepancy. The work can therefore be described as a retained theoretical proposal, but all of its contents cannot confidently be assigned to the April 2024 version. The date inconsistency does not by itself invalidate its technical discussion.

A University of Rochester article dated July 22, 2024 reports NSF-funded research with ELI Beamlines into radiation coherence from electrons interacting with a strong laser field. It presents a gamma-ray free-electron laser as a possible outcome if the underlying science succeeds. This is evidence of a funded research program and its intended direction, not an experimental source demonstration. ELI Beamlines in this account and ELI-NP in the nuclear proposal are separately named platforms and should not be treated as a single experimental program.

The research input also lists a purported iron-57 quantum-model paper by Hausner, Procházka and Vrba, attributed to Physical Review Research 7, 023229 on June 5, 2025, with DOI 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.7.023229. Its supplied INIS link has no captured document or retained text. The review therefore could not verify the reference's identity, the attributed statement about coherent gamma radiation, or the model's implications. This remains an unevaluated research lead; missing source access is not evidence that the paper or its result is false.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied materials document proposals and a dated research program, with no demonstrated device meeting this record's completion criterion. They do not include a bounded freshness-search record supporting the earlier statement that no 2026 experimental coherence result was found. Consequently, the evidence supports the limited account above, but neither a comprehensive absence claim nor a definitive field-wide status assessment as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: produce a beam at MeV photon energy through stimulated nuclear emission or a gamma-ray free-electron-laser mechanism, and publish an interference measurement or a validated spectral measurement that establishes longitudinal coherence and reports its extent. The evidence should connect the measured signal to the emitted gamma radiation and explain how the measurement supports the coherence claim. Brightness, directionality, stimulated gain or spectral narrowing alone would not satisfy this proposal without that connection.
completion_criteria.label: MeV gamma radiation demonstrates longitudinal coherence with measured extent

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: demonstrate operation more than once with the isotope and transition, or electron-source and undulator or laser-interaction settings, stated explicitly. Replacement targets should be allowed where the design consumes or destroys the gain medium; reproducibility need not mean reuse of the same target. Report the conditions and variation between demonstrations so that repeated operation can be distinguished from an isolated signal.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated operation with stated settings and reported variation between demonstrations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical reporting boundary: state photon energy, measured coherence time or length, spectral characteristics, photon yield or flux, beam geometry and relevant operating constraints. Independent reproduction would strengthen confidence in the result. These are proposed criteria for this record, not established community standards. Finite demonstrations establish performance at the tested settings and operating conditions; they do not establish universal coherence across all energies, isotopes or configurations, nor application readiness for spectroscopy or imaging.
completion_criteria.label: Report coherence extent, beam characteristics and relevant operating constraints

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis—PHY-10, Collider-quality plasma wakefield acceleration, has the closest enabling-technology overlap. Both involve demanding control of energetic electrons and strong-field or plasma systems, and advances in electron-beam production could potentially help an electron-based gamma source. The completion goals remain distinct: a coherent gamma source must establish radiation coherence, while collider-quality acceleration concerns beam performance for collisions. Success in either does not establish the other.

Roster synthesis—PHY-02, Sustained net-electric power from controlled fusion, shares a broad high-energy and nuclear-physics context. A coherent gamma source could become an experimental tool for selected nuclear studies if its energy and beam properties are suitable. It would not demonstrate controlled fusion, net electric output or a new power source. PHY-01, Ambient-pressure superconducting conductors at room temperature, is another enabling-materials goal with possible general benefits to scientific equipment, but no necessary dependence between the two breakthroughs is established here.

Roster synthesis—the remaining entries concern distinct discoveries or explanatory tests: PHY-03, A laboratory proof that gravity is non-classical; PHY-04, Laboratory identification of the dark-matter particle; PHY-05, A tested microphysical account of the dark-energy scale; PHY-06, Discovery of a magnetic monopole; PHY-07, Observation of baryon-number violation; PHY-08, Observation of lepton-number violation; PHY-11, A tested resolution of the black-hole information paradox; PHY-12, Experimental identification of the physics that sets the Higgs-mass scale; and PHY-13, A tested mechanism for the cosmic matter excess. A coherent gamma source would be an experimental capability, not evidence for any of these findings by itself. The supplied evidence establishes no specific route from this source to completing those concepts.

unresolved_issues: The iron-57 reference's identity, publication details, attributed statement and relevance remain unverified because no source text was captured.
The discrepancy between the arXiv version header dated April 15, 2024 and the retained body's August 24, 2026 date remains unexplained.
The supplied evidence does not establish whether a qualifying experimental result appeared by November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness-search record was provided.
Figures in the theoretical preprint were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting assessment of claims that would depend on their contents.
No experimentally established coherence extent, operating envelope or application performance for a qualifying source is supplied.
The proposed measurement and reproducibility criteria are not identified as community consensus, and no numerical threshold for useful coherence or application readiness is established.

brief.title: High-energy light whose waves stay in step
possible: Researchers could study how gamma rays, a form of high-energy light, reinforce or cancel each other in controlled experiments. The source would keep the waves in step over a measured time or distance. This alignment is called longitudinal coherence.
why: Physicists would gain a way to control light in a demanding energy range, extending the experimental precision associated with lasers. Longer-term goals include studying atomic nuclei and imaging dense objects.

sources.showed: This is described as a quantum-model paper about iron-57.
sources.cited_for: It identifies a possible theoretical contribution to the study of coherent gamma radiation.
sources.not_established: A quantum model alone would not establish a working source with measured coherence.

sources.who: C.-J. Yang, K. M. Spohr and D. Doria
sources.showed: Their theoretical preprint proposes combining gamma-ray flashes with intense additional light to amplify nuclear emission. Their calculations find that involving several light particles can increase the likelihood of this emission.
sources.quote: We show that multi-photon stimulated emission processes can have a larger effective cross-section compared to a one-photon process.
sources.cited_for: It supports a proposed nuclear route to gamma-ray amplification and explains obstacles that the design must overcome.
sources.not_established: The proposed amplification, target survival and measured coherence have not been demonstrated together experimentally.

sources.who: University of Rochester and ELI Beamlines
sources.showed: They launched a funded research program to study coherence in radiation from electrons interacting with a strong laser field. A gamma-ray laser driven by electrons is a possible eventual outcome.
sources.cited_for: It supports a separate electron-based research route and identifies nuclear studies and dense-object imaging as motivations.
sources.not_established: The program has not demonstrated a reproducible gamma-ray source with the required energy and measured coherence.

shown: Yang, Spohr and Doria have developed theoretical designs for amplifying gamma rays through emission from atomic nuclei. Their preprint describes possible ways around amplification barriers, but reports no working source.

University of Rochester and ELI Beamlines researchers are pursuing a separate route using electrons interacting with an intense laser. Their program aims to establish the underlying coherence before building a source.
missing: A repeatable beam at MeV energies, meaning millions of electronvolts per light particle, with experimentally measured longitudinal coherence.
For the nuclear route, amplification must coexist with target survival and the narrow energy conditions needed for emission.
For the electron route, coherence must be established and carried through into a working source.
Nuclear studies and dense-object imaging need suitable beam energy, output and geometry beyond a coherence demonstration.

milestones.label: Gamma rays demonstrate measurable wave alignment
milestones.explanation: A nuclear or electron-driven source would have to establish longitudinal coherence at MeV energies and measure its duration or length. This would demonstrate the defining capability.

milestones.label: Repeated operation gives documented, comparable results
milestones.explanation: The source would have to work repeatedly, with settings and variation reported; consumed targets could be replaced. This would distinguish reproducible operation from an isolated signal.

milestones.label: Beam performance and operating limits are reported
milestones.explanation: Results would have to report coherence extent, light-particle energy, energy spread, output, beam shape and operating constraints. These measurements would establish what the source delivers under tested conditions.

uncertain: How much coherence would be useful for particular experiments remains undefined.
The proposed measurement and repeatability criteria are not established community standards.
It remains uncertain whether the nuclear designs can amplify radiation while preserving the conditions they need.
